strengths: The core idea is novel and well-motivated: aligning speech tokens with the text transcript at the tokenization stage directly attacks the sequence-length mismatch problem in spoken language modeling, and the authors convincingly position this as the first end-to-end reconstruction-based text-aligned tokenizer.

The method is technically sound and elegantly reuses existing components: initializing the encoder-aggregator from Distil-Whisper (which is already a speech-text aligner) with a cross-attention aggregation over shallow/last encoder representations is a sensible and well-justified design, requiring no explicit word-level alignment.

The tokenization evaluation is convincing: at ~190 bps (roughly 10x lower bitrate than SpeechTokenizer RVQ4), TASTE achieves comparable quality/similarity metrics, and it clearly outperforms the text-only baseline on similarity metrics, showing paralinguistic information is retained despite dynamic sequence-level compression.

Evaluating both a discrete-token variant and a continuous-embedding variant (following MELLE-style latent prediction) strengthens the claim that the text-aligned representation is robust to the modeling paradigm.

Demonstrating that a text LLM (Llama-3.2-1B) can be turned into an SLM with only LoRA fine-tuning is a practically meaningful result, and StoryCloze results (88.9/89.5) substantially exceed both the S3-token baseline and prior work, supporting the claim that text alignment mitigates catastrophic forgetting from the modality gap.
weaknesses: The key SLM comparison baseline (S3 token + LoRA) performs suspiciously poorly (near chance on most SALMON metrics, 63.0 tSC), which makes the headline claim that TASTE outperforms baselines under equal fine-tuning budgets less credible. There is no discussion of why this baseline fails so badly, no tuning of the baseline, and no full-finetuning TASTE result for an apples-to-apples comparison against TWIST/Spirit LM.

Missing ablations for the main design choices: no results with/without the shallow-as-value cross-attention variant, with different ASR initializations, different RVQ depths/codebook sizes, different number of aggregator layers, or the impact of word-level averaging. The method's sensitivity to these choices is unknown.

No evaluation of actual generated speech quality from the SLM. All SLM results are likelihood-based (SALMON anomaly detection, StoryCloze accuracy). For a model intended to 'speak,' perceptual evaluation (MOS, continuation quality by human listeners) or at least objective speech-continuation metrics of decoded generations is needed; how the speaker embedding is selected at inference time for generation is never addressed.

The framing as comparable to full-fine-tuning methods ('perform similarly to previous full-finetuning methods') is a bit overstated: on SALMON, Spirit LM Expr. clearly outperforms TASLM on sentiment/speaker, and the 1B-only model leaves scaling behavior unexplored.

Training data accounting is unclear: how much of the 40,000-hour Emilia English subset was actually used for tokenizer vs. SLM training is not stated, complicating reproduction and fairness of comparison with prior work.

Several notation/consistency errors suggest insufficient polish: Eq. (6) mixes indices i and t; Eq. (10) divides by |L'| while summing over L'; typos throughout (e.g., 'Whipser', 'genearate', 'Consine', 'sopken', 'anomoly', 'druing'); bitrate '~190' is an estimation whose variance across utterances is not characterized.
No code release or reproducibility statement is mentioned, and the compute budget (8xA6000) plus training details, while provided, are not accompanied by artifacts that would allow verification.

Ethical considerations are absent: Emilia contains in-the-wild, pseudo-labeled web-sourced speech including potentially non-consenting speakers, and the paper is silent on data licensing/consent and potential misuse of voice-generating models.

strengths: The core idea of aligning speech tokenization with text at the tokenization stage is well-motivated and directly targets a recognized problem (speech-text sequence length mismatch) in spoken language modeling.

The tokenizer design (ASR-initialized encoder-aggregator with cross-attention aggregation onto text queries) is reasonable and allows text-aligned tokenization without explicit word-level alignment supervision.

The tokenization evaluation covers quality (WER, UTMOS) and multiple similarity aspects (speaker, emotion, duration), and TASTE achieves a remarkably low bitrate (~190 bps) with competitive reconstruction quality.

Evaluating both a discrete token variant and a continuous embedding variant (following MELLE) adds some robustness evidence, and LoRA-based adaptation of a 1B LLM is a practical, efficiency-oriented demonstration.
The paper is generally readable and the method is described in enough detail (losses, quantizer settings, training schedule) to follow.
weaknesses: The headline claim that TASTE-based SLMs 'perform similarly to previous full-finetuning methods' is only weakly supported: on SALMON, Spirit LM Expr. substantially outperforms TASLM on 3 of 4 metrics, and comparisons to prior work (TWIST, Spirit LM, pGSLM) are not controlled for training data, model size, or training budget, making the comparison largely anecdotal.

Evaluation of spoken language modeling relies solely on likelihood-based benchmarks (SALMON, StoryCloze); there is no evaluation of actual speech generation/continuation quality, no listening tests, and no audio samples referenced, so the 'the model can speak' claim is not directly validated.

Missing ablations: no analysis of the number of RVQ layers, codebook size, the aggregator design (shallow vs. last representations), the ASR-initialization choice, or the word-level averaging/aligning procedure; it is unclear which design decisions drive the results.

The method's dependence on ASR transcription quality is a significant practical limitation (errors propagate into tokenization and joint modeling), but the paper assumes 'v is of sufficient quality' and never tests robustness to ASR errors or evaluates on out-of-domain/noisy speech despite training on 40k hours of in-the-wild Emilia data while evaluating only on clean LibriTTS test-clean.

The S3-token baseline in Table 2 performs far below even the ASR+LLM cascade (e.g., 48.8-49.5 on most SALMON metrics), which raises concerns about how the baseline was trained or tuned; without a stronger, fairly tuned baseline, the claimed advantage of text-aligned tokenization for SLMs is not convincingly demonstrated.

Novelty is overstated: combining ASR encoder representations with resynthesis targets is closely related to SpeechTokenizer and CosyVoice's supervised semantic tokens (both cited); the 'first end-to-end approach with a reconstruction objective' claim is contestable and the delta over prior text-aware tokenizers is not crisply articulated.

Bitrate comparisons in Table 1 are somewhat misleading since TASTE's dynamic word-aligned rate is not directly comparable to fixed-rate codecs, and the text-only baseline (~60 bps) serves mainly as a strawman; the duration consistency gap (0.73 vs 0.83-0.88) is acknowledged but underexplored.

No code, model, or tokenizer release is mentioned, limiting reproducibility; the writing contains numerous typos and grammatical errors (e.g., 'genearate', 'druing', 'Consine', 'sopken', 'anomoly'), which suggests insufficient polish.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: the sequence-length mismatch between speech and text tokens is a recognized obstacle in joint speech-text language modeling, and addressing it at the tokenization stage is a sensible and relatively underexplored angle.

The proposed method is technically coherent: initializing the encoder-aggregator from a Transformer ASR model and using cross-attention with shallow encoder representations as values is a reasonable and well-justified design that yields text alignment without explicit word-level alignment supervision.

Strong tokenization results: TASTE achieves comparable or better reconstruction quality (UTMOS 4.25, WER 3.8%) than SpeechTokenizer with RVQ4x1024 while using roughly 10x lower bitrate (~190 vs 2000), which is a genuinely impressive compression result.

Competitive SLM results with an efficient setup: TASLM 1B trained with LoRA achieves strong StoryCloze results (sSC 64.2, tSC 88.9-89.5, exceeding Spirit LM and approaching the ASR+LLM topline), demonstrating that text alignment mitigates catastrophic forgetting of semantic ability with far fewer trainable parameters.

Evaluation covers both tokenization quality (WER, UTMOS, speaker/emotion/duration consistency) and downstream SLM benchmarks (SALMON, StoryCloze), giving a reasonably comprehensive picture, and both a discrete-token and a continuous-embedding variant are explored.
weaknesses: Limited ablation studies: no experiments isolating the contribution of key design choices, such as using shallow vs. last hidden states as values, the number of aggregator layers, the word-level averaging technique, codebook size, or the choice of target unit (S3 tokens). The core mechanism is thus not validated component-wise.

Baseline comparisons are not fully fair or conclusive: the S3-token baseline is trained with what appears to be a substantially simpler joint-modeling setup, and prior works (Spirit LM, TWIST) differ in model size (7B vs 1B) and training data. The underperformance on SALMON relative to Spirit LM Expr. (e.g., sentiment 59.0 vs 73.5, speaker 68.0 vs 81.0) is downplayed rather than analyzed.

Claims of computational savings from reduced sequence length are asserted repeatedly but never quantified with actual training/inference cost measurements (FLOPs, wall-clock, memory), which weakens a headline motivation of the paper.

Heavy dependence on ASR quality and transcripts creates practical limitations that are not discussed: performance on noisy/in-the-wild speech, non-English languages, code-switching, or low-resource languages depends entirely on Whisper transcription quality, and the method cannot be applied to unlabeled speech directly.

The reconstruction setup is somewhat convoluted: TASTE tokens are trained to reconstruct S3 tokens (rather than the raw speech) via an external CosyVoice unit decoder and vocoder, which means the tokenizer is effectively distilled from another tokenizer; this makes direct comparison with tokenizers trained end-to-end on audio (SpeechTokenizer) less straightforward, and this caveat is not clearly acknowledged.

No subjective human evaluation or listening test; the UTMOS score exceeding ground truth (4.25 vs 4.04) is presented as evidence of quality but likely reflects metric artifacts and warrants more cautious interpretation. The duration-consistency gap (0.73 vs 0.83-0.88) is also not deeply analyzed.

Reproducibility concerns: no code or model release is mentioned, several implementation details are underspecified (e.g., lambda_reg/lambda_KL values, exact LoRA target modules, how Emilia pseudo-labels were filtered), and the reported metrics rely on specific off-the-shelf models whose versions matter.

Writing quality needs improvement: numerous typos and grammatical issues throughout (e.g., 'genearate', 'druing', 'Spirt LM', 'sopken', 'Consine scheduler', 'anomoly detector', 'Whipser'), and the appendix algorithm largely restates a trivial grouping/averaging procedure at length.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem formulation: aligning speech tokens with text tokens at the tokenization stage is a clean solution to the length-mismatch problem in joint speech-text spoken language modeling, and the design (Whisper encoder frozen, text-query cross-attention aggregating shallow encoder features, RVQ) is sensible and well-justified.

Extremely low bitrate (~150 bps) while maintaining competitive reconstruction quality and similarity, with a broad set of objective metrics (WER, UTMOS, DNS-MOS, ViSQOL, duration consistency, speaker similarity) plus human MUSHRA tests, and standard deviations reported in the appendix.

Comprehensive SLM evaluation across multiple axes: speech continuation (GPT-4o, UTMOS, human MOS), likelihood benchmarks (SALMON, StoryCloze), and spoken question answering, with a meaningful ablation showing that directly using S3 tokens for joint modeling performs poorly, supporting the paper's central hypothesis.

Impressive efficiency result: a 1.3B-base model with only 45M trainable (LoRA) parameters outperforms 7B SLMs (TWIST, Spirit LM) on speech continuation and StoryCloze, and is the only SLM that improves over its text base LLM on spoken QA.

Interesting demonstration of text-aligned speech editing showing paralinguistic information (duration) is localized in word-aligned tokens; code, demo, and models are released, improving reproducibility.

The appendix candidly discusses related mechanisms (content-style cross-attention in TTS), clarifying the novelty positioning, and the limitation section is honest (no streaming, English-only, no turn-taking).
weaknesses: The tokenizer depends on a large frozen Whisper ASR model at both training and inference, and speech continuation implicitly requires ASR on the prompt to obtain text tokens. This makes the 'end-to-end SLM' claim partially cascade-like and raises questions about robustness to noisy speech, disfluent speech, and non-transcribable audio (music, noise), which are not analyzed.

Comparison fairness is a concern: TASLM is trained on ~40k hours of in-the-wild Emilia plus LibriTTS with text transcripts, while TWIST uses LibriLight without transcripts; differences in training data (scale and domain) confound the attribution of gains to TASTE tokenization. Some evaluated baselines (e.g., baseline S3 token with 45M trainable params) may be under-tuned, making the 'significantly outperforms other pre-trained SLMs' claim somewhat overstated given SALMON acoustic consistency results are actually below TWIST and Spirit LM Expr.

Reliance on LLM-as-judge (GPT-4o) MOS for the semantic evaluation is a relatively weak metric; human MOS is included, which helps, but the GPT-4o scores for all systems (1.37–3.43) have very large variance (±1.3), so differences may not be statistically meaningful.

Uterus-quality metrics exceed ground truth (UTMOS 4.29, DNS-MOS 4.10 vs. 4.09/3.84 for GT) and known limitations of these predictors for reconstruction are not discussed; duration consistency is second-worst, suggesting the dynamic tokenization loses timing fidelity, which is acknowledged but not deeply analyzed.

Novelty is moderate: text-conditioned semantic tokens (CosyVoice S3) and text-speech cross-attention in TTS already exist; the contribution is primarily the combination and its application to joint SLM, which the authors acknowledge. Some ablations (e.g., effect of word-level averaging, R layers, aggregator design choices, shallow-layer choice l) are missing.

Not optimized for streaming/low latency, English-only, and no instruction-following capability; the QA results rely on few-shot prompting and are below larger instruction-tuned systems, limiting demonstrated practical impact.

strengths: The core idea is clean and well-motivated: aligning speech tokens with text tokens at the tokenization stage directly addresses the length-mismatch problem in joint speech-text modeling, and the paper is clear about how this simplifies joint modeling compared to interleaving (Spirit LM) or padding approaches.

The evaluation is multi-faceted: speech reconstruction quality/similarity metrics, a text-aligned speech editing demonstration, speech continuation (human, GPT-4o, UTMOS), likelihood-based benchmarks (SALMON, StoryCloze), and spoken QA, with standard deviations reported in the appendix.

The reported results are competitive: TASLM 1B outperforms 7B baselines (TWIST, Spirit LM) on continuation metrics at much smaller scale, and TASTE achieves very low bitrate (~150 bps) reconstruction.
Reproducibility appears reasonable: training details, hyperparameters, human evaluation protocols, and prompts are provided; demo, code, and models are stated to be released.
The word-level grouping/averaging scheme in Appendix A.2 to handle ASR/LLM vocabulary mismatch is a practical and clearly described contribution.
weaknesses: Heavy reliance on pre-trained components weakens both the novelty claim and the technical contribution: the method depends on Whisper (frozen encoder AND ASR transcription), CosyVoice S3 target tokens, speaker embeddings, and a pre-trained vocoder. The claimed 'end-to-end, no explicit alignment' framing is somewhat misleading since the alignment is effectively outsourced to the Whisper attention maps, and the core mechanism (text-queried cross-attention aggregation) is relatively incremental.

The reconstruction evidence for paralinguistic preservation is mixed and the paper underplays this: TASTE scores second-worst on duration consistency, ViSQOL (3.05) is clearly below fixed-rate codecs (3.3-4.0), and the text-only baseline achieves nearly identical quality metrics at ~50 bps. The MUSHRA gap to the S3 topline and the editing analysis are qualitative/single-example rather than a rigorous quantitative study of paralinguistic transfer.

The 'first to use a reconstruction objective to automatically learn text-aligned tokenization' claim is asserted repeatedly but the related-work differentiation (e.g., vs. SpeechTokenizer, CosyVoice supervised semantic tokens, content-style cross-attention TTS in [3]) is deferred to an appendix and feels thin; the conceptual delta over these prior text-conditioned tokenizers is modest.

The spoken QA comparison (Table 3) is not apples-to-apples: pre-trained-only TASLM with few-shot prompting is compared against instruction-tuned systems (Mini-Omni, Moshi, Llama-Omni), and improvements over the 1B text base are small (24.0->27.1, 51.0->57.6) while remaining far below text models of comparable or larger size.

Several methodological details are unclear or under-justified: the choice of shallow-layer representations as values, the role and weighting of loss coefficients (λreg, λKL), no ablations on RVQ depth, codebook size, aggregator design, or the word-level averaging step; the effect of ASR transcription errors on tokenization quality is assumed away rather than analyzed.

Scope limitations are significant: English-only, non-streaming, no dialogue/turn-taking capability, and the joint modeling is restricted to LoRA fine-tuning of a single 1.3B LLM, leaving generality of the claim across model scales untested.

Some experimental choices weaken claims: GPT-4o-as-judge for semantic continuation with ASR-transcribed audio introduces a circularity with the Whisper-based pipeline, and human tests use only 20 samples per method.

strengths: The core idea—aligning speech tokens to text tokens at tokenization time via a cross-attention aggregator over frozen Whisper encoder representations—is clean, well-motivated, and elegantly sidesteps the length-mismatch problem in joint speech-text modeling without requiring explicit alignment or heuristic interleaving.

Comprehensive evaluation pipeline covering speech reconstruction (objective + human MUSHRA), text-aligned speech editing demonstrations, speech continuation (GPT-4o, UTMOS, and human MOS), likelihood-based benchmarks (SALMON, StoryCloze), and spoken question answering, with standard deviations reported in the appendix.

Strong empirical results for a small model: 1.3B-parameter TASLMs with LoRA (45M trainable) outperform 7B SLMs (TWIST, Spirit LM) on human-evaluated speech continuation, and are the only SLM tested that does not degrade its text base LLM on spoken QA.

Impressive bitrate/reconstruction trade-off (~150 bps) that substantially exceeds the text-only baseline on paralinguistic similarity metrics, plus a novel and intuitive capability of word-level speech editing via token swapping.
Honest related-work discussion (Appendix A.1) distinguishing the contribution from prior cross-attention TTS work, and an explicit limitations section.
Promised release of demo, code, and models supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: Baseline fairness concerns: TASLM is trained on ~40k hours of Emilia plus LibriTTS, while comparisons to TWIST (LibriLight) and Spirit LM may confound data scale/composition with the benefit of text-aligned tokenization; a controlled comparison with matched training data would strengthen the central claim that alignment (not scale) drives the gains.

Benchmark results are mixed: TASLM underperforms TWIST and Spirit LM on several SALMON subtasks (e.g., room/background consistency), so 'comparable performance' claims should be stated more carefully.

Reconstruction quality is not uniformly best: ASR-WER (4.4%) is worse than several higher-bitrate codecs and duration consistency is second-worst, which the paper attributes to dynamic compression but does not analyze or ablate.

The tokenizer depends critically on ASR quality (Whisper transcriptions) and the assumption that last-layer encoder states encode alignment cues; robustness to transcription errors, noise, non-English speech, and failure modes is unexamined.

Small human evaluation (20 samples per method, 10+ raters) and reliance on GPT-4o-as-judge for semantic MOS introduce potential statistical and validity concerns; confidence intervals for MOS differences are not tested.

The SQA comparison mixes instruction-finetuned systems with a few-shot pretrained model, and results on WebQuestions (27.1) trail much larger systems considerably, limiting the strength of that claim.

Minor writing issues (e.g., 'a attention', 'the the', 'druing', 'Consine', 'protocal') and some ambiguity in the relationship between the token-level (Eq. 6) and embedding-level (Eq. 8) TASLM variants, including which is preferable and why.
No ablation over key design choices such as which encoder layers are used as keys/values, number of RVQ layers, or the effect of word-level averaging on reconstruction quality.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: the text-speech length mismatch in joint spoken language modeling, addressed elegantly at the tokenization stage via text-aligned speech tokens (TASTE), enabling straightforward one-to-one joint text-speech modeling without heuristic interleaving or padding.

Technically clean method: cross-attention aggregation over frozen Whisper encoder layers (last layer as keys, shallow layer as values) is simple, well-justified, and end-to-end with no explicit alignment module; the design choices are supported by ablations (Table 4) and CCA analysis (Figure 6).
Impressive efficiency: ~150 bps, ~3 Hz token rate while achieving on-par or better reconstruction quality than much higher-bitrate codecs (Table 1), plus strong noise robustness (Table 8).

Comprehensive evaluation: reconstruction metrics, human MUSHRA and continuation MOS tests, GPT-4o-based semantic evaluation, likelihood benchmarks (SALMON, StoryCloze), spoken QA, and several ablations (ASR effects, layer selection, attention visualizations, standard deviations reported). The 1.3B TASLM outperforming 7B SLMs on continuation is a notable result.

Strong additional demonstrations such as text-aligned speech editing via token swapping, and few-shot spoken QA that preserves base LLM text capability — evidence that the design principle (tokens carry paralinguistic rather than lexical content) works in practice.
Good reproducibility posture: code, models, and demos released; detailed training hyperparameters and evaluation protocols in the appendix.
weaknesses: Bitrate/efficiency comparisons are somewhat apples-to-oranges: TASTE delegates lexical content to the text side, so its ~150 bps cannot be directly compared with codecs (Encodec, Mimi, BigCodec) that encode full speech including content; the text-only baseline already beats TASTE on WER/UTMOS/DNS-MOS, so the quality advantage over low-rate codecs partly reflects this decomposition rather than better codec design.

Baseline comparability in Table 2 is not fully controlled: TASLM is LoRA-finetuned from LLaMA3.2-1B with the authors' data (Emilia+LibriTTS), while comparisons (TWIST, Spirit LM) differ in base model, training data, and full fine-tuning; the 'Baseline (S3 token)' setup appears to use a 45M model which is hard to interpret. Claimed superiority over 7B SLMs should be tempered by these confounds.

Dependence on ASR quality is a structural limitation: TASTE tokens are bounded by transcription quality, which affects applicability to noisy, multilingual, or non-lexical speech; the ASR ablations mitigate this for clean-ish conditions but the limitation section acknowledges narrow scope (English only, single-speaker, no overlapping speech).

Novelty is moderate: text-speech cross-attention for fine-grained control exists in TTS (Chen & Rudnicky 2022), and aligning speech with text representations has been explored elsewhere; the main contribution is the framing and system-level demonstration that text-aligned tokenization improves joint SLM modeling, rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

Likelihood-based results are competitive but not uniformly best (SALMON background/room attributes notably weaker; overall behind Spirit LM Expr. in one configuration), and the GPT-4o semantic evaluation protocol is known to be noisy despite the secondary-ASR ablation.

strengths: The core idea—aligning speech tokens one-to-one with text tokens at the tokenization stage to eliminate the length mismatch in joint text-speech modeling—is clearly motivated and cleanly executed via a cross-attention aggregator over frozen Whisper encoder representations.

TASTE achieves remarkably low bitrate (~150 bps vs. thousands for codec baselines) while maintaining competitive reconstruction quality, supported by both objective metrics and a MUSHRA human listening test.

The evaluation is broad: speech reconstruction, speech continuation (GPT-4o, UTMOS, human MOS), likelihood-based benchmarks (SALMON, StoryCloze), few-shot spoken QA, module ablations, ASR-error ablations, noise-robustness experiments, CCA analysis justifying the shallow-layer choice, and attention-map visualizations.
Standard deviations are reported for the main tables, human evaluation protocols and prompts are disclosed, ASR-induced errors are explicitly ablated (Tables 5-7), and code/models/demo are released.
The text-aligned speech editing demonstrations provide intuitive qualitative evidence that tokens carry paralinguistic rather than lexical information.
weaknesses: Comparisons in Table 2 are confounded: TASLM is LoRA-fine-tuned from LLaMA3.2-1B (a much stronger recent base LM), while the outperformed 7B SLMs (TWIST, Spirit LM) are built on LLaMA-2/OPT. The claimed '1.3B outperforms 7B SLMs' advantage may largely reflect base-LM strength and fine-tuning regime rather than the tokenization itself; the only jointly trained baseline under identical conditions is the weak S3-token baseline.

The SLM comparison relies on a single self-trained joint-modeling baseline (S3 token); no other joint text-speech tokenization schemes (e.g., SpeechTokenizer-style distillation, Mimi-based joint modeling, GLM-4-Voice-style reduced-frequency tokens) are trained and evaluated under the same setup, weakening the central claim that text-aligned tokenization is the key factor.

The tokenizer requires the text transcription as input at inference, making the whole pipeline dependent on ASR quality for any speech input (e.g., continuation prompts, downstream speech understanding); while the ASR ablation shows small degradation on LibriSpeech, behavior on accented, noisy, or out-of-domain speech is only partially addressed by the white-noise robustness study.

Novelty is moderate: aligning speech tokens to text via ASR encoders/attention has close precedents (SpeechTokenizer's ASR distillation, cross-attention fine-grained TTS control the authors themselves cite, reduced token-frequency approaches in Moshi/GLM-4-Voice); the contribution is a recombination of known components (Whisper encoder, cross-attention, RVQ, S3 units, LoRA), and the paper overstates the 'first end-to-end' framing.

The word-level grouping/averaging/replication scheme (Algorithm 1) to bridge ASR-LLM vocabulary mismatch is a heuristic patch that partially undermines the clean 'one-to-one alignment' story, and its effect is not ablated.

Human evaluations use only 20 samples per method (10+ scores each), and the continuation-MOS comparisons between systems with large per-sample variance (±1.2-1.4) rest on a small sample set; the MUSHRA test also deviates from the ITU protocol by omitting the low-pass anchor.

On SALMON, TASLM underperforms prior work on acoustic-consistency tasks (e.g., Spirit LM Expr. notably better on sentiment/speaker/gender), which the paper attributes to training data but does not fully resolve; the 'overall' average mixing semantic and acoustic benchmarks is of questionable value.

Several presentation issues remain: typos ('the the', 'druing', 'Seciton', 'MUSRHA'), an underspecified choice of l=6 appearing only in the appendix, and the claim of 'extensive experiments' when the SLM scale (1.3B) and language coverage (English only) are limited.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem formulation: the paper identifies the length-mismatch/modality-gap problem in joint text-speech modeling and addresses it at the tokenization stage rather than with post-hoc interleaving or padding heuristics, which is a genuinely useful design perspective for spoken language modeling.

Technically clean method: text-aligned tokenization via cross-attention aggregation (text as query, deep encoder states as keys, shallow states as values) is simple, end-to-end, requires no explicit forced alignment, and yields a dynamic, very low token rate (~3Hz, ~150 bps).

Comprehensive and multi-faceted evaluation: reconstruction quality/similarity metrics, MUSHRA human listening tests, speech continuation (GPT-4o, UTMOS, human MOS), likelihood-based benchmarks (SALMON, StoryCloze), few-shot spoken QA, plus extensive ablations (module-wise, shallow-layer selection via CCA, ASR error impact, noise robustness, alternative ASR for evaluation). Standard deviations are reported, which is commendable.

Strong empirical results: a 1.3B LoRA-finetuned TASLM outperforms 7B pretrained SLMs (TWIST, Spirit LM) on speech continuation across human and machine evaluation, and the text-aligned tokens enable precise, word-level paralinguistic speech editing, providing convincing evidence for the central claim.
Reproducibility support: training details, hyperparameters, prompts, word-level vocabulary-mismatch algorithm, and a stated release of demo, code, and models.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate and partly incremental: the core ingredients (frozen Whisper encoder, RVQ, S3-style units, flow vocoder, text-speech cross-attention as in Chen & Rudnicky 2022) are largely existing components; the contribution is primarily their combination and the text-aligned reformulation. The 'first end-to-end approach' claim may be contested given related alignment-based tokenizers (e.g., leveraging ASR encoder representations in Du et al., 2024a).

Architectural dependence on ASR: tokenization requires a high-quality transcription from a frozen Whisper encoder, tying the tokenizer to ASR quality and complicating streaming/low-latency use (acknowledged only briefly in limitations). Reconstruction similarity (ViSQOL, speaker sim.) is still below the S3 topline, showing a real information-loss trade-off.

Scope of evaluation is narrow: English-only, evaluation on LibriSpeech test-clean, relatively modest training data (~40k hours), and comparison baselines use different base LLMs and training regimes (full pretraining vs. LoRA), so some cross-model comparisons are not fully controlled.

Evaluation reliability concerns: GPT-4o-based semantic MOS is a noisy proxy; human listening tests use only 20 samples per condition; continuation baselines are evaluated 'under their own decoding schemes,' introducing potential confounds in the headline Table 2 claims.

Writing has minor errors and some overclaiming (e.g., 'intriguingly find out', section cross-references like '§2.1.1' mismatching numbering), and the significance of the spoken QA result is somewhat underdeveloped given the few-shot setup.
